title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Secret
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Maya pressed her hand against the cold, salt-crusted door of the lighthouse. Nobody had opened it in years, or so the fishermen said. Her grandfather had kept the light burning for thirty seasons before he vanished one stormy October night, and the door had been locked ever since.

The key, warm from being clutched in her fist the whole walk down, trembled slightly as she turned it. The lock gave way with a groan that seemed to echo up through the spiral staircase above her. Dust swirled in the thin blade of afternoon light that slipped through the doorway, and for a moment Maya hesitated, her heart thudding against her ribs.

"You don't have to do this," her brother Theo called from the path behind her, though he made no move to stop her either.

Maya didn't answer. She had spent five years wondering what her grandfather had been guarding, why he refused to let anyone else near the lantern room, and why the last thing he had said to her was, 'Keep it lit, no matter what.' She stepped inside.

The staircase wound upward into shadow, each step creaking beneath her feet like it, too, was waking from a long sleep. At the top, the lantern room was exactly as she had imagined it a hundred times: a great glass lens, taller than she was, sitting silent and dark in the centre of the room. But it was the small, weathered logbook on the windowsill that made her breath catch. She opened it carefully, and there, in her grandfather's careful handwriting, was an entry dated the very night he disappeared.

title: Guardians of the Reef
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species on Earth. In the waters around the Cayman Islands, reefs provide a home for parrotfish, sea turtles, and the elusive Nassau grouper, as well as protecting the coastline from powerful waves during hurricane season.

A coral reef is not a rock, as many people assume, but a living structure built by thousands of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp produces a hard, cup-shaped skeleton, and over hundreds of years these skeletons stack together to form the reef we see today. Some of the largest reef systems took thousands of years to grow to their current size.

Unfortunately, reefs around the world are under threat. Rising sea temperatures cause a process called coral bleaching, where stressed coral expels the colourful algae living inside it, turning the coral white and weak. If temperatures do not cool again quickly, the coral can die completely. Pollution, overfishing and careless snorkelling or diving can also damage reef ecosystems.

However, there is hope. Marine parks, such as those protecting large sections of Cayman's coastline, restrict fishing and anchoring in sensitive areas. Volunteers and scientists have also begun 'coral gardening' projects, growing new coral fragments in underwater nurseries before transplanting them onto damaged reefs. Every visitor who avoids touching coral and every diver who follows marine park rules helps to protect these fragile underwater cities for future generations.

title: Trade Winds
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
The trade wind combs the palm trees flat,
And flicks white lace across the bay,
It whistles through the fisherman's net
And carries salt spray far away.

It does not pause for anyone,
Not boat, nor bird, nor beating drum,
It only knows the path it's run
Since long before the tourists come.

At dusk it settles, soft and low,
A breath held gently over sand,
As if the whole wide ocean's glow
Were resting lightly in its hand.

title: Adrift
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
The engine spluttered twice, coughed once, and died. Priya turned the key again — nothing but a dry click. Above them, the sky that had been clear an hour ago was now the colour of a fresh bruise, purple-grey and swelling fast.

"We need to get back," said Kai, gripping the side of the small boat as it rocked beneath them. "Now, Priya."

"I'm trying!" She turned the key a third time. The engine gave a half-hearted groan and fell silent again. Out here, halfway between the reef and the shore, there was no one to call for help — their radio had been left charging on the kitchen counter that morning, a mistake Priya was already regretting.

The first fat raindrops began to fall, striking the water like tiny stones. Kai reached for the oars stowed beneath his seat, his hands trembling slightly as he fitted them into place. "We'll row. It's not that far."

Priya wasn't so sure. The current here was strong, and the wind was already dragging the boat sideways, away from the safe curve of the bay and towards the darker, rockier stretch of coastline beyond it. She said nothing, not wanting to frighten him further, and instead grabbed the second oar.

They rowed in silence, matching each other's rhythm, as the rain thickened around them and the shoreline blurred into a smear of green and grey. Twice, a wave slapped hard against the hull and sent cold spray across their backs. Priya's arms burned, but she didn't stop.

Then, through the curtain of rain, she saw it: the old fishing shack at the edge of the bay, its tin roof catching what little light remained. It wasn't home, but it was shelter, and right now, that was all that mattered.

"There!" she shouted, pointing. Kai followed her gaze, and without a word, they both dug their oars deeper into the water.

title: Voyager's Long Goodbye
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
In 1977, two small spacecraft called Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer planets of our solar system. Neither was expected to survive for more than a few years. Nearly fifty years later, both are still travelling — and both have now left the solar system entirely, making them the most distant human-made objects in the universe.

Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 used a rare planetary alignment, which happens only once every 176 years, to visit Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, using the gravity of each planet to slingshot themselves onward to the next. Along the way, they sent back the first close-up photographs of Jupiter's giant red storm and Saturn's icy rings, transforming what scientists understood about the outer planets.

Each spacecraft carries a Golden Record, a phonograph disc containing sounds and images chosen to represent life on Earth: whale songs, laughter, greetings in fifty-five languages, and music from around the world. Scientists included it in case the spacecraft is ever found by another civilisation, though nobody expects that to happen for millions of years, if ever.

Today, Voyager 1 is more than 24 billion kilometres from Earth, so far away that a radio message takes over 22 hours to reach it. Both spacecraft are now travelling through interstellar space, the vast region between stars, and are gradually running out of power. Engineers on Earth have begun switching off their scientific instruments one by one to conserve the last of their energy, hoping to keep at least one instrument working into the 2030s.

Even when the Voyagers finally fall silent, they will not stop travelling. Long after Earth's sun burns out, the two spacecraft will still be drifting silently among the stars, carrying their golden record of a civilisation that once sent them on their way.

title: The Old Fig Tree
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Before the road was paved in grey,
before the houses came to stay,
I stood alone on open land,
my roots sunk deep in golden sand.

I watched the fishermen walk by,
their nets flung wide against the sky,
I watched their children climb my arms,
and shelter safe from island storms.

Now cars go by both day and night,
new buildings block the morning light,
but still the old men stop and stare,
and say, 'That fig tree still stands there.'

I do not mind the change of years,
the new-built shops, the engineers,
for every child who climbs today
still hears the same wind pass this way.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean Seas
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
For more than a century, from the 1650s to the 1730s, the Caribbean Sea was one of the most dangerous stretches of water in the world. Pirates roamed between its islands, attacking merchant ships loaded with sugar, silver and other valuable cargo travelling between Europe and the Americas.

Contrary to popular legend, most pirates were not searching for buried treasure. Gold and silver coins were usually spent quickly in port on food, repairs and supplies, rather than buried on remote beaches. Instead, pirate crews were often more interested in practical goods: cloth, tools, medicine and, above all, food and fresh water for the long voyages ahead.

Life aboard a pirate ship was, in some surprising ways, fairer than life in the official navies of the time. Many pirate crews elected their own captain and could vote to remove him if he made poor decisions. Stolen goods were often divided according to agreed shares, with injured crew members sometimes receiving extra payment as a form of early compensation for their injuries.

The Cayman Islands, with their many hidden coves and shallow reefs, provided useful shelter for ships avoiding storms or naval patrols during this era. Sailors passing through sometimes stopped to hunt turtles for food, which is how the islands are thought to have earned an early reputation among passing sailors as a useful stopping point along Caribbean trade and pirate routes.

By the 1730s, most piracy in the Caribbean had been stamped out. Naval forces grew stronger, more organised, and better equipped to hunt down pirate ships, while several governments offered pardons to pirates willing to give up their lawless life. The era of Caribbean piracy left behind countless legends — some true, many exaggerated — that continue to capture people's imaginations to this day.

title: The Vanishing Painting
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
The painting had hung in the school hall for as long as anyone could remember: a faded portrait of the school's founder, Elizabeth Hartley, staring sternly down at generations of nervous students queuing for assembly. On Monday morning, it was simply gone, leaving nothing behind but a pale rectangle on the wall where it had hung for over a hundred years.

"Someone must have taken it over the weekend," said Mr. Okafor, running a hand through his hair as he studied the empty space. "The caretaker locked up as usual on Friday, and everything was normal then."

Priya crouched down and examined the wall more closely. A thin scratch ran along the skirting board just beneath where the painting had hung, as though something heavy had been dragged rather than carried. She glanced towards the fire exit at the end of the corridor — the emergency door that was supposed to be alarmed.

"The alarm didn't go off though," said Kofi, following her gaze. "If someone had used that door, we'd have heard it."

"Unless," Priya said slowly, "they didn't use the door at all." She pointed upward, to the low ceiling tiles of the corridor, one of which sat very slightly askew, as if it had recently been disturbed and not quite replaced properly.

Mr. Okafor frowned. "You think someone came through the ceiling? That seems rather elaborate for a school painting."

"Maybe it's not just an old painting," Priya replied. She had noticed something the others hadn't: a small, neat label visible in the pale rectangle's corner, reading 'Property of the National Gallery, on loan.' Whoever had taken the portrait of Elizabeth Hartley clearly knew exactly what it was worth — and exactly how to disappear with it.

title: Should Homework Be Banned?
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Every evening, millions of children around the world sit down after a full day at school to complete more schoolwork at home. But is homework actually helping students learn, or is it simply taking away precious time that children could spend playing, relaxing or being with their families? It is time to seriously reconsider whether homework, especially for younger students, is doing more harm than good.

Firstly, research suggests that for primary-aged children, the benefits of homework are extremely limited. Unlike older students preparing for exams, young children generally learn best through play, conversation and hands-on activities — not through repeating worksheets at the kitchen table after a long day. Forcing tired children to complete extra written tasks in the evening can lead to frustration, arguments at home, and a growing dislike of school itself.

Secondly, homework is not fair to every family. Some children have quiet bedrooms, helpful parents and a reliable internet connection; others do not. A student without these advantages is placed at an unfair disadvantage compared to a classmate with a calm, well-resourced home to study in — through no fault of their own.

Of course, supporters of homework argue that it builds good habits, such as responsibility and independent learning, that will help students later in life. There is some truth to this, particularly for older students. However, these same skills could easily be built during the school day itself, through carefully designed independent tasks, without placing extra pressure on family evenings.

For these reasons, schools should seriously reduce or remove homework for younger students, replacing it instead with a strong recommendation to read for pleasure each evening — an activity proven to support learning without the stress.

title: The Woman Who Mapped the Ocean Floor
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
For most of human history, people believed the bottom of the ocean was flat, featureless and largely unknown. That changed thanks to the painstaking work of an American scientist named Marie Tharp, who spent years transforming scattered depth measurements into the first detailed map of the entire ocean floor.

In the 1940s and 1950s, women were rarely permitted to work as scientists aboard research ships, so Tharp instead worked at a desk, carefully studying the sonar readings her male colleagues collected at sea. Sonar works by sending sound waves down through the water and timing how long they take to bounce back off the seabed, revealing how deep the ocean is at that point.

As Tharp plotted thousands of these measurements by hand, she noticed something remarkable: a long, deep valley running down the centre of a vast underwater mountain range called the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. She believed this valley, known as a rift valley, was evidence that the ocean floor was slowly splitting apart — a radical idea at the time, since most scientists still believed the continents never moved at all.

When Tharp first shared her theory, many colleagues dismissed it as impossible, some even calling it "girl talk." It took years of further evidence, collected by other scientists exploring the same ridge, before Tharp's map and her theory were finally accepted. Today, her rift valley discovery is recognised as key evidence supporting plate tectonics, the theory explaining how the Earth's continents slowly drift over millions of years.

Marie Tharp's ocean floor maps, first published in the 1970s, are still used as the foundation for modern seafloor charts. Her careful, patient work — turning columns of numbers into a picture of a world nobody had ever seen — changed how scientists understood the entire planet.
